items.title: Representative Jimmy Gomez Resigns After House Ethics Panel Finds Evidence of Sexual Misconduct
items.standfirst: Gomez is the second Democrat from California to resign from Congress this year following sexual misconduct allegations.
items.content: Representative Jimmy Gomez, a Democrat from California, during a House Intelligence Committee hearing on worldwide threats in Washington, D.C, on March 19, 2026. —Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg—Getty ImagesRepresentative Jimmy Gomez, a California Democrat, announced his resignation Monday after a House ethics panel found “substantial evidence” that he engaged in sexual misconduct.Gomez, in a statement, said he “recognize[s] the seriousness of the Ethics Committee’s report,” but has “strong disagreements” with its conclusions. “Among other significant deficiencies and omissions, the report does not include key portions of my testimony that are essential to a full and fair understanding of what occurred,” Gomez said.He also criticized the process of the investigation, which began after a report of him kissing an aide emerged in April. “With this in mind, I see no other alternative than to resign, effective December 1, to allow for my staff to close out important constituent casework and needs,” he added.Gomez has represented California’s 34th district since 2017, after winning a special election to succeed Xavier Becerra, who at the time was appointed the state's Attorney General after Kamala Harris was elected to the Senate. Gomez was already set to leave office in early 2027, after losing his re-election bid to newcomer Angela Gonzales-Torres.But his resignation just weeks before the congressional turnover would make Gomez the second California Democratic lawmaker to resign from his congressional seat this year amid sexual misconduct allegations. In April, former Representative Eric Swalwell, who was then eyeing the governor’s seat and had Gomez as his campaign co-chair, resigned days after allegations of his sexual misconduct surfaced.Congress has faced renewed scrutiny over its apparent failures to stop abuses of power and to police inappropriate behavior following a spate of sexual misconduct allegations leveled against its members.The House ethics panel earlier this year also found that Republican Representative Chuck Edwards of North Carolina acted inappropriately toward staffers. Edwards’ colleagues voted to censure him, following the panel’s recommendations. Ahead of the vote, Edwards wrote a six-page letter to other House members defending himself. Representative Cory Mills, a Florida Republican, also faces an ongoing ethics probe over allegations of sexual and financial misconduct. Mills, who has denied the allegations, lost a primary election earlier this year.Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader set to be Speaker after Congress flipped blue, said in a joint statement with his fellow party leaders that the report on Gomez was “serious and deeply troubling” and that his resignation was “appropriate.” The leaders added that “decisive action to set a new standard for reform is an urgent priority for House Democrats,” as they take over Congress next year.What were the allegations against Gomez?While Swalwell’s controversy made headlines in April, the New York Post reported that Gomez was seen “surreptitiously kissing a much younger congressional aide in the summer of 2023.” According to the report, the incident happened outside a backyard party hosted by Swalwell “to celebrate the start of the August congressional recess.”Gomez had resigned as co-chair of Swalwell’s California gubernatorial campaign after the allegations against his colleague emerged, which he called “shocking.”According to the Ethics Committee’s report, on May 6, Gomez, who is married, disclosed through counsel that he had “a past consensual, sexual relationship with a senior employee in the personal office of a more senior Member of Congress,” and “one sole occasion” of “consensual kissing with a senior employee of another, more senior Member’s office.”The ethics panel reached out to both female employees. The first denied nonconsensual sexual interactions with Gomez. But the second female employee, who was in her mid-20s and worked in the House for years before leaving in 2025, told the committee that she had more than one physical encounter with Gomez, both of which she did not consider consensual.The woman first met Gomez in 2018, but had little interaction with him, according to the committee report. She had her first “meaningful interaction” with Gomez at a Feb. 29, 2024 birthday party hosted by another congressional member in a bar near Capitol Hill. She and Gomez left the party with the unspecified lawmaker and another unidentified woman for a Chinatown bar.According to the report, the woman told the panel that while they were at the Chinatown bar, Gomez started to touch her legs, adding: “he put his hand down my skirt and then put his fingers inside of me.” She said the incident was nonconsensual.Later outside the bar, the woman said Gomez pushed her against a wall and kissed her, and she said she “kissed him back because I just wanted to go home and I just, like, wanted it to end.” Gomez, according to the report, recalled that he made sexual contact with the woman only once they were outside the bar. The second encounter happened in July 2024, according to the woman. She told the panel that during an evening vote series in the House, she texted Gomez and met up with him at his office upon his invitation. They talked, but she eventually felt uncomfortable and made a motion to leave, but as she was about to leave, Gomez tried to kiss her in a “pretty forceful” manner.“I opened the door, and he grabbed my arm and he, like, grabbed my body and, like, pushed it into his and started caressing my back and, like, put his hand on my face and, like, tried to kiss me,” she said. Gomez testified that he had walked her to the door and bid her goodbye, to which the woman reacted “fine.” He also told the panel that he did not try to kiss her on the lips; that besides a hug, he did not put his hands on her; and that no signs showed her discomfort with the interaction.The panel found that the interactions with the former female employee “constitute sexual misconduct in violation of House Rules and merit consideration by the full House.” The committee report said that Gomez’s conduct “at various junctures suggests he knew that what he was doing was wrong,” and that his actions towards her “could implicate D.C. laws related to criminal sexual assault, including misdemeanor sexual abuse.” But the committee did not recommend any punishment for Gomez, citing his re-election loss.What are the reactions?Lawyers for the woman at the heart of the allegations against Gomez lauded the Ethics Committee for its handling of the investigation.“However, Representative Gomez’s conduct did not occur in a vacuum, and immediate steps must be taken by Congress to rein in what the report describes as a ‘toxic and predatory culture,’” her attorneys Lisa J. Banks and Sarah E. Nesbitt said in a statement. “Democracy cannot function properly when women must endure harassment and abuse as a condition of public service.”Gonzales-Torres, who defeated Gomez in the midterms, criticized him for not resigning sooner and told the Los Angeles Times on Monday that the accusations against him “reflect a broader environment of sexual misconduct and toxic working conditions on Capitol Hill.” Last week, the House Ethics Committee adopted rule changes to fast-track and improve transparency related to sexual misconduct probes, amid pressure brought on by the increase in allegations.Representative Teresa Leger Fernández of New Mexico, who chairs the Democratic Women’s Caucus, called Gomez’s actions “reprehensible and a gross abuse of power” and thanked the Ethics Committee for its investigation, which forced the embattled California lawmaker to resign instead of facing a motion to expel him from the chamber. GOP Representative Kat Cammack of Florida, who, alongside Leger Fernández, co-chairs the bipartisan task force aimed at changing the way Congress handles sexual harassment claims, said that while resigning is the “right call,” it cannot “begin and end” there.“This is bigger than one member,” Cammack said. “Misconduct and toxic working conditions still fester in too many offices on Capitol Hill, and we can’t keep responding after the fact.”

items.title: 6 Questions About Jensen Huang's Stunning Return as Nvidia CEO
items.standfirst: Just 11 days after resigning amid an alleged espionage scandal, Huang is back at Nvidia—with questions swirling about Trump's intervention, national security, and the future of the AI industry.
items.content: Jensen Huang and Donald Trump on Sept. 29, 2026 in Washington, D.C. —Kevin Dietsch—Getty ImagesEleven days. That’s how long it took Jensen Huang to return to his post of CEO of Nvidia after resigning in the wake of an alleged espionage scandal that rocked the business, tech, and policy worlds. On Nov. 12, Huang stepped down from the company he co-founded in 1993 after acknowledging an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese national whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected was a Chinese spy. Her former company, Megaspeed, is also under criminal investigation over possible export-control violations. (The two Huangs are not related.)But on Monday, Nvidia’s board announced that it had unanimously reinstated Huang after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his reinstatement “poses no national security risk.” Donald Trump personally claimed credit for the reversal, telling CNBC that “I convinced them” and “I made the deal.”The stock market surged, with Nvidia shares rising more than 30% as trading opened Monday. The broader market has now recovered more than half of last week’s plunge, temporarily easing fears that an AI slump could lead to a recession. But Nvidia and Huang still face an uncertain and treacherous path forward. Here are six big questions about his return. What role did Trump play in Huang’s return? Just a week ago, the NVIDIA board made it clear that it intended to turn the page on the Huang era. At the company’s Q3 earnings call on Nov. 17, chairman Harvey Jones told investors that the board did “not intend to reinstate Huang,” despite the fact that the former CEO was angling for a return.The board had plenty of reasons to not want him back. Reuters reported that Huang had misled several company leaders about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. Separate reports emerged alleging that Jensen Huang had relationships with two Nvidia employees, including Kimberly Powell, a vice president who reported to him.But the board also faced intense pressure to reinstate him. An online campaign attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including from executives like Elon Musk and people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees. And most centrally, President Trump said Monday that he personally intervened. Trump told CNBC that he had spoken to Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly,” and that Vice President JD Vance was also involved in discussions. On Monday morning, Trump indicated to a reporter that he knew Huang would be reinstated before the news broke.Notably, the board reinstated Huang before completing its independent investigation. Directors said a series of meetings had satisfied them about Huang’s “candor and ability to lead,” and that senior government officials had assuaged their national-security concerns. They did not identify those officials or explain what information they supplied.The swift about-face has provoked questions even from Republicans. "Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” wrote Utah Senator John Curtis. What did U.S. intelligence actually find?It remains unclear what U.S. intelligence discovered about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang—and how damaging its findings were. The New York Times reported Sunday that Alice Huang remained in contact with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 through the fall of 2026—a period overlapping with her affair with Jensen Huang.But the intelligence community has not publicly established that she knowingly acted as a spy, and Beijing has denied the allegation. Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday that Attorney General Todd Blanche did “not possess evidence” that Huang engaged in unlawful conduct. However, a slew of questions remains unanswered. Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence, said on Sunday that an investigation into Alice Huang and her firm Megaspeed was ongoing. And more reporting continues to be published about the complex relationships between Megaspeed, the Chinese government, and various Chinese AI companies. Bloomberg, for instance, reported that a company founded by Alice Huang procured Nvidia chips installed at a Shanghai data center connected to the Megaspeed network.How will the move impact the Trump administration and U.S. export policies? The Nvidia scandal has exacerbated deep fissures within the Trump administration over China. More laissez-faire members of the administration, exemplified by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, are happy with Nvidia selling some of its chips to China, which they argue is good for U.S. business interests and keeping China hooked on American technology. But the Nvidia scandal empowered a competing faction of China hawks, who argue that Trump should take a more adversarial stance. Four days after Huang resigned, the Commerce Department issued a rule intended to close a major loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access restricted American chips remotely through data centers in third countries.With Huang back in charge at Nvidia, the balance could tip back in his favor.How will Nvidia respond internally? The scandal has also revealed cracks within Nvidia, the world’s top chip supplier. It’s no secret that Huang has always been the culture-setter for Nvidia and its hard-charging, relentless work ethic. But recent reporting, especially from the Times, alleges that Huang crossed a line into public humiliation, threats, and verbal abuse. Now that Huang is back, will his power be checked—or unleashed? The board, in its statement, stressed more oversight, including a new committee of independent directors that will oversee national-security and export-control risks, and a chief compliance officer who reports to a board committee. But Huang has now survived a seemingly insurmountable crisis with the support of the president and other Silicon Valley power players. That could make him more difficult to restrain, in a manner similar to how Sam Altman returned to OpenAI with a reconstituted board that left him more powerful than before his ouster.Lindsey Stewart, director of institutional insights at Morningstar, an investment research company, says that the fact that Huang was reinstated before his investigation was concluded “is going to add to those corporate governance questions that investors have"—especially given that the company is "exposed to several material risks." What congressional scrutiny will Huang and Nvidia face?As Huang resumes the role of helming one of the biggest companies in the world, he will also be pulled away from his desk to Washington to answer questions from irate policymakers. He has agreed to a transcribed congressional interview on Dec. 1 before the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs, and China committees, and has also been asked to appear on Dec. 3 in a public Senate hearing.That scrutiny will likely increase in January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. Many Democratic candidates ran on platforms of accountability and rooting out corruption. Lawmakers have already demanded that the administration preserve records involving Nvidia, Megaspeed, Huang’s communications with Trump, and the government’s export-control decisions. “Congress must get to the bottom of what’s going on at Nvidia. Jensen Huang must testify under oath,” Congressman Greg Casar wrote in a statement on Monday. Investigators may also examine Trump’s financial interest in Nvidia. Public disclosures show that he bought between $1 million and $5 million of Nvidia stock in the days before his administration rescinded a Biden-era chip rule in May 2025, and made at least three additional purchases shortly after announcing that Nvidia could sell H200 chips to China. White House representatives have stated that Trump’s holdings are managed by independent advisors.What does this episode mean for the AI economy? Huang’s return stopped the stock market bleeding on Monday. Longterm, his presence could be enormously beneficial to an industry that critics feared was on the verge of bursting. Huang has long played the role of AI’s chief investor, salesman, and diplomat. But his return also revealed how concentrated the entire American economy has become—and could provoke a larger backlash from a public that already is skeptical of AI leadership and how much power they hold. A survey from Athena Insights last week found that more than half of respondents oppose Huang’s return, and believe the affair to be a serious national security issue.“From the standpoint of both democracy and healthy financial markets, no one person should wield that kind of influence,” says Aya Ibrahim, Senior Fellow at the AI Now Institute.
